messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The call had come in as a standard collision on the I-95 overpass, but when Arjun arrived, a ruptured tanker had split its silver cargo across the wet asphalt. The air felt heavy, coated in the sharp, medicinal sting of industrial solvent that clung to his throat and seeped through his gear. He remembered kneeling beside the overturned cab, pressing his hands against the driver’s chest, feeling that same acrid taste on his lips. In that moment, terror had arrived fully formed, a cold weight in his ribs. Years later, the smell of alcohol at a neighborhood gathering would instantly pull him back to that overpass, the chemical bite replacing the present entirely. His workplace, once a place of routine, became saturated with the same quiet dread. For weeks after, Arjun found himself trapped by memories that struck without warning. When they returned, they arrived as full sensory waves, the terror identical to what he had breathed at the scene. He would have to stop whatever he was doing, grip a doorframe, and wait until the emotional tide receded. He could not linger on the details. What frightened him most was the certainty that he should have known better—that if he had only called for additional ventilation before removing his respirator, the cloud could have been dispersed. The rumination became a relentless loop. He replayed the radio chatter and the exact angle of the truck, searching for a single decision that, if changed, would have rewritten the outcome. He knew the mental calculus would never stop. As the memories and the rumination occupied his days, Arjun found he needed to stay constantly surrounded. At the station, he lingered in the kitchen, volunteered for extra shifts, and made sure he was never alone in the bunk room. He kept his phone ringing, his mouth busy with casual talk, because silence meant the overpass would return unannounced. His days as a paramedic gradually narrowed to administrative duties and dispatch desk work, a deliberate distance from the very rigs that once defined his career. The avoidance of ambulances and hospital corridors meant he stopped volunteering for community health outreach, and his team began to notice his quiet withdrawals during morning briefings. His wife noticed how he flinched when he passed the fire station parking lot, how he suddenly became unavailable whenever an ambulance siren faded past their house. He had long ago stopped scheduling routine physicals, unable to sit in examination rooms where the sterile antiseptic felt too familiar, or watch paramedics load a patient without his pulse spiking. Avoiding the workplace, the dark corners of the station, and any medical cue became an automatic routine. At sixty-one, Arjun finally stepped into a clinic because the constant socializing had frayed his sleep, and his wife’s persistence had outlasted his resistance. He sat in the chair, hands folded tightly over his knees, bracing for the familiar dread of speaking the event aloud. What he wanted most was to quiet the terror that followed the memory, to stop treating every dark hallway and every faint chemical scent like a returning threat. What he feared was that the incident had permanently altered how his mind read the world. He hoped, for the first time, that sitting in this quiet room might teach him how to stop waiting for the past to catch up to him.
